1. Identification Strategy
- Primary: Sharp regression discontinuity design (RDD) at the Democratic two-party vote margin cutoff of zero. Treatment is the Democrat barely winning the general election; control is the Democrat barely losing. Outcomes include next-cycle party success (vote share and win probability), as well as mechanisms (e.g., spending, challenger quality, CQ ratings).
- Complementary: Local randomization RD within a narrow bandwidth, treating observations inside the window as if randomized. This provides design-based balance tests on rich pre-determined covariates.
- Secondary (for mechanism decomposition): Within a tight window around zero, model the probability of bare victory as a function of pre-election covariates (CQ ratings, candidate experience, fundraising, gubernatorial/SoS partisanship) to assess whether “as-if random” holds and to describe mechanisms pushing a candidate over the top.
- Optional RD-IV: For estimating a candidate incumbency advantage, use bare victory in t as an instrument for being the incumbent candidate in t+1 within an RD window, with flexible controls for the running variable on each side.

Why this works here:
- The institutional rule induces a known, deterministic cutoff at 50% of the two-party vote for seat allocation. Near the cutoff, the assignment of seat control is plausibly as-if random absent precise manipulation.
- The dataset is tailored to this design, with corrected outcomes, rich pre-determined covariates (including CQ race ratings), and long time span to support precision, bandwidth choice, and extensive validity checks.


2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable: Democrat wins the House general election in district d, year t. Treated = 1{Dem two-party margin at t > 0}.
- Control group: District-elections where the Democrat barely loses at t (Dem margin just below 0).
- Treatment timing/event date: Election day in year t (general election). Outcomes measured contemporaneously (seat control) and in t+1 (next general election, typically t+2 years).
- Running variable and cutoff: Running variable is the Democratic two-party vote margin m_dt = DemShare2pty_dt − 0.5 (in proportion units). Cutoff c = 0. Treatment assigned when m_dt ≥ 0.
- Outcomes for main estimand: 
  - Reduced-form party advantage: Dem win at t+1; Dem two-party vote share at t+1; Dem incumbent presence at t+1; campaign finance outcomes at t+1; challenger quality at t+1.
  - Optional IV estimand: Effect of being the incumbent candidate (t+1) on Dem outcomes (instrumented by bare victory at t).


3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff: In the absence of treatment (seat assignment), the conditional expectation of outcomes varies smoothly with the Dem margin at 0. With rich pre-determined covariates, this implies balance of CQ ratings, prior terms, lagged vote share, fundraising, normal presidential vote, demographics at the cutoff.
  - Plausibility: Strategic entry and national tides select which races are close, but RD only requires smoothness within the very narrow neighborhood. We will test this by checking continuity/balance in pre-determined covariates and lagged outcomes.
- No precise manipulation of the running variable around the cutoff: Actors cannot sort exactly to the winning side of zero.
  - Plausibility: Questionable due to recounts, selective mobilization, and discretionary decisions in razor-thin races. We will address with a donut RD that removes the ultra-close range where recounts are most likely (e.g., |margin| < 0.5–0.75 pp), and with local randomization balance tests.
- SUTVA/local variation: No other discontinuity at m = 0 except party control of the seat (e.g., recount rules do not change discretely exactly at 0). 
  - Plausibility: Automatic recount thresholds are based on absolute margins, not sign; they also do not generally occur exactly at zero. We mitigate with donut exclusions near common recount thresholds and by testing for discontinuities in recount exposure if available.
- For RD-IV (if used): Exclusion and monotonicity. Bare victory affects next-cycle outcomes only via incumbency status of the candidate (or via party’s control of the office), and there are no “defiers.”
  - Plausibility: Exclusion may be strained if winning at t changes other determinants of t+1 outcomes beyond incumbency (e.g., party investments), so we prefer reduced-form RD for party outcomes and use RD-IV cautiously for candidate-level incumbency.


4. Threats to Identification and Mitigations
- Recounts/administrative discretion and last-minute GOTV near the threshold (manipulation at m ≈ 0):
  - Mitigations: 
    - Donut RD: exclude |m| below 0.5–0.75 pp (sensitivity to values).
    - Density test (rddensity) just outside the donut; estimate separate RDs on each side of recount-likely bands.
    - Local randomization window selected to pass balance on many pre-determined covariates; randomization-inference p-values.
- Imbalance in pre-determined covariates due to professionalized campaigns (CQ ratings, incumbent experience, fundraising):
  - Mitigations:
    - Test continuity/balance for all available pre-determined variables (including lagged outcomes). If specific covariates are unbalanced, include them in covariate-adjusted RD (rdrobust with covariates) and conduct Oster/partialling sensitivity.
    - Explicitly model mechanisms: within very tight windows, regress win on pre-determined covariates to quantify predictability; if predictability remains high, report local randomization results using a narrower window where balance holds.
- Redistricting between t and t+1:
  - Mitigations:
    - Exclude cases where boundaries change between t and t+1 using the redistricting indicator.
    - Robustness: include them with controls for redistricting and test that results are similar; also look at t+3 outcomes (same redistricting cycle) as a robustness check.


5. R Code Outline
Note: This is a template; adapt variable names to your file. Assumes proportions for shares.

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(dplyr)
library(rdrobust)
library(rddensity)
library(fixest)   # for flexible regressions
library(AER)      # ivreg if using RD-IV

# 1) Load data
# Expected columns (rename as needed):
# state, district, year, dem_share_2pty, dem_win (0/1), 
# redistrict_next (1 if boundaries change before next election),
# cq_rating_dem (higher=more D-favorable, pre-election),
# prior_house_terms_dem, prior_house_terms_rep,
# spend_dem, spend_rep (nominal), donate_dem, donate_rep,
# normal_pres_vote_dem (district presidential normal vote),
# gov_dem (state governor is Dem), sos_dem (SoS is Dem)
dt <- fread("house_elections_1942_2008.csv")

# 2) Basic constructs
dt <- dt %>%
  mutate(
    dist_id = paste(state, district, sep = "-"),
    dem_margin = dem_share_2pty - 0.5,            # running variable (proportions)
    treat_demwin_t = as.integer(dem_margin > 0),
    log_spend_ratio = log((spend_dem + 1) / (spend_rep + 1)),
    log_donate_ratio = log((donate_dem + 1) / (donate_rep + 1))
  ) %>%
  arrange(dist_id, year) %>%
  group_by(dist_id) %>%
  mutate(
    year_lead1 = lead(year),
    dem_share_lead1 = lead(dem_share_2pty),
    dem_win_lead1 = lead(dem_win),
    # Example endogenous next-cycle variable: Dem incumbent candidate at t+1
    dem_incumbent_cand_t1 = lead(treat_demwin_t),  # proxy: D won at t implies D incumbent candidate at t+1
    redist_next = lead(redistrict_next)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # keep regular general elections with next general at +2 years
  filter(!is.na(year_lead1), year_lead1 == year + 2)

# Sample restriction: exclude redistricting between t and t+1
main <- dt %>% filter(redist_next != 1 | is.na(redist_next))

# 3) Manipulation/density test (outside a donut to avoid recount issues)
# Define a donut exclusion width (in proportion units): 0.005 = 0.5 percentage points
donut_w <- 0.005
dens_samp <- main %>% filter(abs(dem_margin) > donut_w)
dens <- rddensity(X = dens_samp$dem_margin)
summary(dens)

# 4) Reduced-form RD: Effect on Dem win in t+1 (party advantage)
# Main outcome: dem_win_lead1
# Use rdrobust with donut and cluster by district
rf_samp <- main %>% filter(!is.na(dem_win_lead1), abs(dem_margin) > donut_w)

# RD without covariates
rd_rf <- rdrobust(y = rf_samp$dem_win_lead1, x = rf_samp$dem_margin, c = 0, kernel = "triangular", vce = "nn", cluster = rf_samp$dist_id)
summary(rd_rf)

# RD with rich pre-determined covariates (covariate-adjusted RD)
covs <- rf_samp %>% 
  select(cq_rating_dem, prior_house_terms_dem, prior_house_terms_rep, 
         normal_pres_vote_dem, log_spend_ratio, gov_dem, sos_dem) %>% 
  as.matrix()

rd_rf_cov <- rdrobust(y = rf_samp$dem_win_lead1, x = rf_samp$dem_margin, covs = covs, c = 0, kernel = "triangular", vce = "nn", cluster = rf_samp$dist_id)
summary(rd_rf_cov)

# 5) Reduced-form RD on Dem vote share at t+1
rs_samp <- main %>% filter(!is.na(dem_share_lead1), abs(dem_margin) > donut_w)
rd_share <- rdrobust(y = rs_samp$dem_share_lead1, x = rs_samp$dem_margin, c = 0, kernel = "triangular", vce = "nn", cluster = rs_samp$dist_id)
summary(rd_share)

# 6) Placebo/balance tests at cutoff for pre-determined variables and lagged outcomes
# Example: CQ rating and lagged Dem vote share (t-1)
bal_samp <- main %>%
  arrange(dist_id, year) %>%
  group_by(dist_id) %>%
  mutate(dem_share_lag1 = lag(dem_share_2pty)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(abs(dem_margin) > donut_w)

rd_bal_cq <- rdrobust(y = bal_samp$cq_rating_dem, x = bal_samp$dem_margin, c = 0, kernel = "triangular", vce = "nn", cluster = bal_samp$dist_id)
summary(rd_bal_cq)

rd_bal_lagshare <- rdrobust(y = bal_samp$dem_share_lag1, x = bal_samp$dem_margin, c = 0, kernel = "triangular", vce = "nn", cluster = bal_samp$dist_id)
summary(rd_bal_lagshare)

# 7) Local randomization approach (optional): choose a window that balances covariates
# Here, pick a tight window and do difference-in-means with FE standard errors
lr_w <- 0.02  # 2 percentage points
lr <- main %>% filter(abs(dem_margin) <= lr_w, abs(dem_margin) > donut_w)
feols(dem_win_lead1 ~ treat_demwin_t, data = lr, cluster = ~ dist_id)

# 8) Mechanism analysis: Predict bare victory within a tight window
mech_w <- 0.02
mech <- main %>% filter(abs(dem_margin) <= mech_w)
# Logistic/probit; we’ll use logit via fixest
mod_mech <- feglm(treat_demwin_t ~ 
                    cq_rating_dem + prior_house_terms_dem + prior_house_terms_rep +
                    log_spend_ratio + normal_pres_vote_dem + gov_dem + sos_dem +
                    factor(year),
                  data = mech, family = "binomial")
summary(mod_mech)

# 9) Robustness checks:
# - Alternative donut widths and bandwidths
donut_w2 <- 0.0075
rf_samp2 <- main %>% filter(!is.na(dem_win_lead1), abs(dem_margin) > donut_w2)
rd_rf2 <- rdrobust(y = rf_samp2$dem_win_lead1, x = rf_samp2$dem_margin, c = 0, kernel = "triangular", vce = "nn", cluster = rf_samp2$dist_id)
summary(rd_rf2)

# - Covariate-adjusted linear RD via fixest with interactions in margin by side (within an h)
# Use rdrobust to pick bandwidth and then run a parametric check
bw <- rd_rf$bws[1]  # left bandwidth (use max of left/right for symmetry)
h <- max(rd_rf$bws[1], rd_rf$bws[2], na.rm=TRUE)
param <- rf_samp %>% filter(abs(dem_margin) <= h)
param <- param %>% mutate(post = as.integer(dem_margin >= 0))
feols(dem_win_lead1 ~ post + dem_margin + post:dem_margin +
        cq_rating_dem + prior_house_terms_dem + prior_house_terms_rep + 
        normal_pres_vote_dem + log_spend_ratio + factor(year),
      data = param, cluster = ~ dist_id)

# 10) (Optional) RD-IV for candidate incumbency advantage at t+1
# Build kernel weights from rdrobust bandwidth h and triangular kernel
w <- with(rf_samp, {
  h_use <- h
  k <- (1 - abs(dem_margin)/h_use) * (abs(dem_margin) <= h_use)
  k
})
# Instrument dem_incumbent_cand_t1 with treat_demwin_t, controlling for margin piecewise linear
rf_samp$w <- w
iv_mod <- ivreg(dem_share_lead1 ~ dem_incumbent_cand_t1 + dem_margin + I(dem_margin * (dem_margin >= 0)) |
                              treat_demwin_t + dem_margin + I(dem_margin * (dem_margin >= 0)),
                data = rf_samp %>% filter(abs(dem_margin) <= h),
                weights = w)
summary(iv_mod)
```


6. Expected Results
- Comparability at the cutoff: I expect most pre-determined covariates (CQ ratings, prior experience, lagged vote share, normal presidential vote, demographics) to be statistically smooth at zero after excluding the ultra-close recount window and redistricted cases. Nevertheless, some residual predictability of the winner from CQ/spending within very tight windows is plausible.
- Causal advantage of a bare win for the party in the next election (reduced form):
  - Next-cycle probability of winning (party holds the seat): positive and sizable, roughly +0.15 to +0.25.
  - Next-cycle vote share: positive, roughly +0.05 to +0.08 (two-party share).
- Mechanisms: Higher subsequent fundraising and presence of a same-party incumbent candidate are likely channels; CQ ratings in the next cycle should shift favorably for the party that barely won at t.


7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
- C1: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff supported by balance in rich pre-determined covariates (after donut and no-redistricting filter): 1
- C2: No precise manipulation of the running variable at the cutoff (density smoothness; recount/admin discretion do not induce sorting): 0
- C3: Robustness to bandwidth/polynomial choice and kernel; consistent results across rdrobust and parametric checks: 1
- C4: No other discontinuities at the cutoff (e.g., policy rules) affecting outcomes; donut excludes recount-impacted margins: 1
- C5: Placebo tests on predetermined variables and lagged outcomes show no discontinuity: 1

Notes
- The primary estimand is the reduced-form causal effect of seat control assigned at t on party performance at t+1, identified via sharp RD. 
- RD-IV for candidate incumbency is optional and requires stronger exclusion. If used, interpret carefully and report both reduced-form and 2SLS.
- Report full covariate balance tables and density plots; pre-register bandwidth choices and donut thresholds, then show sensitivity to alternatives.
